property_summary: For every call to fallback, the reference contract accepts only calls that send exactly 10 ether (calls with value == 10 ether succeed), whereas the mutant inverts that check and thus will reject exactly-10-ether calls and accept others (so there exists some value — e.g. 10 ether — where the mutant's acceptance differs); the test fuzzes the sent amount and asserts that for all inputs the reference accepts iff value == 10 ether (we implement by asserting that the reference's fallback call succeeds exactly when the sent amount equals 10 ether).

For every call to C.fallback with some msg.value and advancing time, the reference contract always accepts (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant inverts that check and will reject exactly-10-ether calls (so there exists an input amount where acceptance differs).

For any call to C.fallback, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant inverts that check and will reject exactly 10 ether and accept others, so there exist amounts where acceptance differs.

For every call to C.fallback, if the sent msg.value equals 10 ether then the reference C will transfer its entire balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0 (after accepting the call), but the mutant inverts the value check and will reject exactly-10-ether calls so there exist inputs (msg.value == 10 ether at a block where block.number % 15 == 0) where the reference sends the contract balance to the caller while the mutant does not accept the call and therefore does not send the balance.

For every call to C's fallback, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant inverts that check (requires msg.value != 10 ether) so there exist amounts (notably 10 ether) where the mutant's acceptance differs from the reference.

Invariant: any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp such that block.timestamp >= pastBlockTime after the call (i.e., fallback requires block.timestamp to be strictly greater than the previous pastBlockTime), whereas the mutant requiring block.timestamp < pastBlockTime breaks this (there exist inputs where the mutant's require allows different ordering and will revert or violate the relation).

For any call to fallback with exactly 10 ether, the contract's pastBlockTime after the call is equal to the current block.timestamp (and thus block.timestamp >= previous pastBlockTime when the call succeeds); the mutant inverts the time comparison and will reject many advancing-timestamp calls or behave inconsistently, so there exist fuzzed timestamps/blocks that make the mutant fail where the reference succeeds.

For any caller and any time/block, a call to fallback with exactly 10 ether on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) when block.timestamp is >= previous pastBlockTime after advancing time, while the mutant that requires block.timestamp < pastBlockTime will reject many otherwise-valid advancing-timestamp calls — so the correct contract accepts calls that advance time, but the mutant can revert for such inputs.

For any caller and any timestamp increase, if a call to fallback is made with exactly 10 ether and block.timestamp is strictly greater than the contract's stored pastBlockTime, the reference contract's fallback succeeds and updates pastBlockTime to the new timestamp; the mutant inverts the comparison and will revert for such advancing timestamps (so there exist fuzzed timestamps/blocks where the reference accepts the call but the mutant rejects it).

For any caller and any block timestamp, when calling fallback with exactly 10 ether and the block timestamp strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime, the reference contract accepts the call and updates pastBlockTime to the new timestamp (so the call succeeds), whereas the mutant that inverts the comparison will revert for such advancing timestamps — there exist fuzzed timestamps and block numbers demonstrating this difference.

For any caller and timestamp, after calling fallback with exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp increases, the reference contract stores pastBlockTime equal to block.timestamp; the mutant that assigns pastBlockTime = block.number will violate this for some inputs (when block.timestamp != block.number).

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later block.timestamp than the stored pastBlockTime, the reference contract always records pastBlockTime equal to block.timestamp afterwards; the mutant that stores block.number instead will violate this whenever block.timestamp != block.number (which holds for many inputs).

For any caller, when calling fallback with exactly 10 ether at a strictly later timestamp than the previous call, the reference contract only empties its balance (transfer to caller) on blocks where block.number % 15 == 0; the mutant changes the divisor to 16 so there exist inputs (block.number values) where the mutant transfers but the reference does not (or vice versa).

For any caller and any block timestamp strictly greater than the previous stored pastBlockTime, a fallback call that sends exactly 10 ether always leaves the contract balance equal to (previous balance - possibly zero if transfer forwarded because block.number % 15 == 0) but more generally the reference contract sometimes forwards its entire balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0, whereas the mutant never forwards balance — therefore there exists inputs (block.number such that %15==0 and caller with 10 ether) where address(c).balance decreases in the reference but not in the mutant.

For every call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any caller at a strictly later block timestamp, the reference contract sometimes forwards its entire balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance becomes 0 in that case), while the mutant never does; therefore the universal rule: if block.number % 15 == 0 and msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime then address(c).balance == 0 after the call — the reference satisfies this for all such inputs, the mutant violates it for those inputs.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to fallback at a strictly later timestamp, when the block number is a multiple of 15 the reference contract will forward its entire balance to the caller (leaving address(c).balance == 0) while the mutant that removed the conditional transfer will not, so asserting address(c).balance == 0 after such a call distinguishes them.

For any valid call to fallback that advances time, the reference contract only transfers its entire balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance becomes 0 exactly when block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant performs an unconditional drain after each qualifying call, violating that rule for some blocks where block.number % 15 != 0.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether and with timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract only drains its balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0, whereas the mutant unconditionally drains the balance after updating pastBlockTime (so for some block numbers not divisible by 15 the mutant will make address(c).balance == 0 while the reference keeps it > 0).

For any valid fallback call (msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) the reference contract only drains its entire balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0; the mutant unconditionally drains the balance for every qualifying call, so there exist block numbers not divisible by 15 where the mutant makes address(c).balance == 0 but the reference keeps it > 0.

For any valid fallback call (msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) the reference contract only drains its balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0, so address(c).balance remains nonzero after a qualifying call when block.number % 15 != 0; the mutant unconditionally drains the balance after updating pastBlockTime, violating this by making address(c).balance == 0 for some inputs where block.number % 15 != 0.

For every call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and executes (i.e., msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime), the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp before any conditional transfer (so address(c).balance becomes 0 iff block.number%15==0), whereas the mutant that defers the assignment can cause the transfer to use the old pastBlockTime outcome and thus lead to a different post-call pastBlockTime or balance for some inputs.

For every valid call sending exactly 10 ether and with block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference C always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp before performing the conditional transfer (so after the call, pastBlockTime == the call's timestamp), while the mutant that moves the assignment after the transfer can leave pastBlockTime unchanged for calls where the transfer triggers (block.number % 15 == 0) if that transfer drains funds or reverts, causing pastBlockTime to differ from the call timestamp for some inputs.

For any caller and any timestamp/chain state where a fallback call with exactly 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime completes (does not revert), the correct contract always sets pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp after the call (i.e. the getter pastBlockTime equals the call's timestamp), whereas the mutant can cause pastBlockTime to remain unchanged for some inputs when the conditional transfer triggers (block.number % 15 == 0) and interacts badly with a malicious recipient.

For every admissible call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any caller and at any time where block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, C always ends the call with pastBlockTime equal to that call's timestamp (the reference updates pastBlockTime before any transfer), whereas the mutant that moves the assignment after the conditional transfer can be made to leave pastBlockTime unchanged by forcing the conditional transfer to attempt to send to a contract that reverts, causing the fallback to revert in the mutant or to behave differently; thus the property is that after a successful fallback call pastBlockTime == the call timestamp for all admissible inputs.

For any fallback call that sends exactly 10 ether and where the call completes successfully, the reference C always sets pastBlockTime to the call's block.timestamp (so pastBlockTime == block.timestamp after the call); the mutant that moves the assignment after the conditional transfer can be made to revert the transfer (via a malicious recipient) or otherwise alter control flow so that for some inputs the call still completes but pastBlockTime does not equal the call timestamp, breaking the rule.
